en.title: Company rule, Permanent Settlement, and Darbhanga Raj
en.summary: The East India Company acquired fiscal authority in Bihar before it created representative institutions or a modern public administration. That sequence matters. From the grant of the dīwānī in 1765 onward, the Company's first durable claim on villages, markets and landed houses was a claim to revenue. Courts, policing, survey, registration and bureaucratic classification expanded around that fiscal core.

outline: : the dīwānī and a new revenue sovereign
The limits of the 'dual government' shorthand
The famine of 1770 and the fiscal state

en.title: Agrarian society, markets, caste, and labour
en.summary: The agrarian history of Mithila, Vajji-country, and Anga cannot be reconstructed from the image of an isolated, self-sufficient village. Periodic markets, fairs, ferries, river ports, roads, railway stations, pilgrimage centres, credit networks, and seasonal migration connected cultivators and labouring households to district towns, Patna, Bengal, Nepal, Assam, and wider commercial circuits. Anand A.

en.title: Rivers, calamity, transport, and the colonial state
en.summary: Colonial rule in north Bihar and the eastern Ganga plain encountered a landscape in which rivers altered fields, roads, ferries, administrative boundaries, and taxable assets. The state answered with surveys, flood reports, embankment files, railway engineering, remission rules, relief codes, and district statistics. These records make environmental change unusually visible, but they were produced for government purposes and must be read as interventions as well as descriptions.

Bagmati, Kamla, Gandak and the multiplicity of flood regimes

en.title: Education, print, language, reform, and nationalism
en.summary: Tols, pathshalas, maktabs, Persianate instruction, household teaching, temple- and monastery-linked learning, occupational apprenticeship, and courtly scholarship all predated the spread of colonial schools. The nineteenth century therefore did not introduce education into an intellectual vacuum. It altered the institutions through which learning could be certified, financed, inspected, and converted into employment.

en.title: The Nepal Tarai, Rana rule, and the border to 1951
en.summary: The Nepal Tarai was never merely an empty frontier awaiting settlement from the hills. Forests, grasslands, wetlands, farms, market towns, pilgrimage centres, estates, and older settlements linked the Himalayan foothills to the Gangetic plain. Its history therefore has to begin with inhabited landscapes and competing claims, not with the administrative language of reclamation.
